data.source_title: Inter-organizational pooling of NICU nurses in the Dutch neonatal network: a simulation-optimization study
data.locator: Section 2, operational-bed analysis; Section 3, model assumptions; Table 6 operational capacity occurrence.
data.source_setting: Nine-location Dutch national NICU network; operational-bed counts were self-reported through BabyZoektBed and depend on available nurses, physical beds, and patient acuity.
data.source_period: Operational-capacity empirical input: 2020; demand estimates: 2015-2019; simulation outcomes generated in 10-year steady-state runs with 10 replications and a 1-year warm-up.
data.source_n: Nine NICUs; 2020 operational-capacity input distribution summarized across network locations. Site-specific availability was not published for privacy reasons.
data.quantity: Empirical occurrence of weekly staffed operational capacity as share of maximum capacity
data.unit: percent of weeks in the study input distribution
data.source_evidence_basis: The model used a one-year 2020 empirical distribution of self-reported operational capacity; for example, 80% of maximum capacity occurred in half of observations. Authors also report individual NICUs had no operational bed available on average 53% of the time, with up to 82% at the most occupied site, but do not disclose the sites.
data.limitations: Dutch network and 2020 capacity conditions; self-reported source data, rounded input frequencies, site identities suppressed. The 1:2 nurse-to-bed ratio elsewhere in the model is an explicit simplifying assumption and should not be interpreted as a staffing standard. Neither capacity values nor results are RWJ observations.
data.inferred_scenario_use: Distinguish licensed/physical beds from operational staffed capacity and make capacity acuity-sensitive; only use this as an external model-design prompt, not as a numeric local calibration.

data.source_title: Inter-organizational pooling of NICU nurses in the Dutch neonatal network: a simulation-optimization study
data.locator: Section 4.3, baseline and flex-pool experiment results; Figures 6-10.
data.source_setting: Discrete-event simulation and integer-linear-program optimization of staffing and patient allocation across nine Dutch NICU locations; scenario pool shares nurses across organizations.
data.source_period: Empirical capacity input year 2020, patient-demand inputs 2015-2019; 10-year steady-state simulations with 10 replications after a one-year warm-up.
data.source_n: Nine NICU locations; simulated network-wide annual transport counts estimated from model output, not a patient-level study cohort.
data.quantity: Modeled annual patient transports under baseline vs five-flex-nurses-per-location, all-location sharing scenario
data.unit: percent of simulated patients and approximate transports/year
data.source_evidence_basis: In the model, five flex nurses per location with all nine locations participating reduced predicted patient transports by about 70%; the authors report mean 6.31% (95% CI 5.63%-6.98%) versus baseline 21.53% (95% CI 20.46%-22.60%). This is a modeled scenario, not observed intervention effect.
data.limitations: Results depend on Dutch geography, staffing-sharing feasibility, assumed shift timing, acuity and LOS inputs, and objective weights; model assumes patients/staff shift only at shift boundaries although real neonatal transfers occur through the day. The authors note real-world short-term capacity mitigations (such as moving infants to lower-care units) are not fully modeled. Not a local forecast or RWJ result.
data.inferred_scenario_use: Use the model structure to test whether operational nurse capacity, acuity, referral acceptance, network transfers, and step-down/discharge transitions should interact; do not import its effect size or assumptions as a local prediction.
